nodes.title: The Lantern Ferry Won't Wait

academicTarget.skill: math.multiplication.transfer — equal groups, missing factor, and word-problem interpretation applied to unseen contexts and unseen number pairs

nodes.mechanic: Loading run: the child fills ferry decks by choosing how many crates go in each row and how many rows, then sends the ferry across a river that is rising; each departure is timed by the water level, not a clock.
nodes.theme: A night river crossing during a flood. Lanterns must reach the far village before the water swallows the dock. The child is the loader on the last ferry of the night.

openingScreen.title: The Lantern Ferry Won't Wait
openingScreen.purpose: The first screen shows the dock already ankle-deep and one ferry left, with a dockmaster saying only: "Sixty lanterns. Eight to a crate. Tell me how many crates and I'll start hauling." No tutorial, no practice round — the child's first act is a real load decision that the ferry departs with.

generationPrompt.text: Build a five-crossing loading run for a nine-year-old on unseen multiplication transfer. Each crossing gives a total and one known part of the grouping, and the child must supply the missing part before the ferry can leave. Crossing 1: total lanterns and lanterns-per-crate given, child states crate count. Crossing 2: crates and per-crate given, child states total, but the deck only fits a set number of rows so the child must arrange as rows × columns. Crossing 3: a word problem where the dockmaster mentions two numbers that beg to be added ("nine villagers waiting, each needs four lanterns") — the correct move is multiplication. Crossing 4: a total that factors more than one way (e.g., 36) with a constraint that only one factor pair satisfies ("crates must fit six across the ramp"), so a memorized pair is not enough. Crossing 5: the deck grid is hidden under a tarp — no objects to count, the child must reason the missing factor from total and rows alone, with larger numbers than any earlier crossing. Every answer is committed by dragging the crate stack onto the ferry; once it's aboard, the ferry leaves. Capture each response verbatim, unassisted, with latency. No hints before commit; after a wrong crossing the dockmaster says what actually arrived and what didn't, then the water rises and the next crossing begins. Assignment: Festival Team Challenge. Academic construct to preserve: Lab Learner can produce correct multiplication answers on rehearsed material; whether that reflects transferable equal-groups and missing-factor reasoning is untested, and will show most clearly when a total admits multiple factor pairs and only a situational constraint selects the right one. This node must test unseen transfer: change the context while preserving the construct. Author fresh items. These have already been seen and must not be reused verbatim: math.multiplication.equal_groups, math.multiplication.missing_factor, math.multiplication.word_problem_interpretation. Planner decision behind this node: All three baseline observations were unassisted and correct (accuracy 1.00, above the preregistered 0.70–1.00 band), and the predicted factor-pair overgeneralization never surfaced. But every item was tagged exposure=previously_practiced and provenance=practice, so this is rehearsed performance, not transfer. Practice cannot confirm the hypothesis; it can only justify the transfer test. Quest eligibility is met on independent correct evidence, so the correct move is to spend that eligibility on genuinely unseen material — missing-factor and equal-groups reasoning embedded in a situation the child has never met, where a factor must be recovered rather than recalled. The 43-second completion and 5/5 rating also say the baseline was too small to strain anything; the Quest should cost something. Created at: 2026-08-08T19:10:33.597Z.

design.stakes: Lanterns are the stake and they are spent, not scored. Every crossing the child under-loads, those lanterns stay on the dock and the flood takes them — the far village stays dark in that district, visibly, for the rest of the run. Over-load and the ferry swamps: the crates that sink are gone too. The child is playing to see how much of the village they can light, and the ending screen is the far shore as they actually left it — five districts lit, or three, or one. A wrong answer costs real, permanent, visible territory. It does not end the run, because the run's point is the shape of the shoreline at the end, and a child who lost district two should still be fighting for district five.
design.failureMode: A run can end with the far village mostly dark. If three or more crossings are mis-loaded, the water reaches the dock before the fifth ferry and the last crossing never happens — the run ends early, with the remaining lanterns shown floating away and a count of how many people are still waiting in the dark. That is a real loss and it is presented as one.
design.escalation: Crossing 1 is a clean total-and-part with a visible grid to check against. Crossing 2 adds a deck constraint so the grouping must be arranged, not just counted. Crossing 3 hides the multiplication inside language that invites addition. Crossing 4 makes the total ambiguous so a memorized factor pair fails without the constraint. Crossing 5 removes the visible objects entirely and raises the numbers past anything earlier — reasoning only, with the water at the child's knees and one ferry left.
design.mechanicSpec: The child drags a crate stack from the dock onto the ferry deck; a number pad sets crates-per-stack and a slider sets stack count, and the running lantern total is shown only as crates aboard — never as the answer. Tapping "Cast off" commits. On a correct load the ferry pulls out, the far shore lights up one district at a time as crates unload, and the water level drops a notch. On an under-load the ferry leaves anyway with a gap on the deck, the leftover crates are shown on the dock, and the flood pulls them into the current while the corresponding district on the far shore stays black. On an over-load the deck tilts, crates slide off the stern and sink with the lanterns going out one by one underwater. After every crossing the water line on screen rises by a fixed amount; at three failures it crosses the dock boards and the run ends there.
design.mathematicalHook: Thirty-six lanterns can be crated as 4×9, 6×6, or 12×3 — the arithmetic is equally true every way, and the ramp width is what decides which truth loads the ferry. The whoa is discovering that a number has several shapes, and the situation, not the multiplication table, picks the one that fits.

nodes.title: Forty-Two Fireflies and One Wrong Jar

academicTarget.skill: math.multiplication: synthesis of equal-groups construction, missing-factor reasoning, and word-problem interpretation on unseen totals whose multiple factor pairs are disambiguated only by a stated physical constraint

nodes.mechanic: Constraint-locked jar packing: the child drags a fixed swarm of fireflies into jars, choosing how many jars and how many per jar, then survives a constraint that invalidates all but one arrangement.
nodes.theme: A night-shift firefly keeper loading glow-jars onto a lantern cart before the swarm's light fades. The cart, the shelves, and the swarm all have rules, and the rules do not care what is easiest to multiply.

openingScreen.title: Forty-Two Fireflies and One Wrong Jar
openingScreen.purpose: The first screen shows 42 fireflies drifting in one glass dome and an empty cart with three shelves. One line: "Every jar on this cart must hold the same number. Fill them all, or the light dies before the cart reaches the bridge." No tutorial — the child's first act is a grouping decision, and it is already the measurement.

generationPrompt.text: Build a three-round packing instrument for a 9-year-old. Round 1: 42 fireflies, child sets jar count and fireflies-per-jar by dragging; the cart accepts only arrangements where every jar is equally filled and no firefly is left in the dome. Multiple pairs work (2×21, 3×14, 6×7, 7×6, 14×3, 21×2), so let the child commit freely — then reveal the cart shelf holds exactly 6 jars and re-run their choice against it. Round 2: 56 fireflies, the shelf constraint is stated up front as "7 jars, all equal" — the child must reason to the missing per-jar count, and the jars visibly overflow or sit half-lit if wrong, spilling fireflies that fly off and shrink the swarm. Round 3: a written order from the bridgekeeper — "I need 9 lanterns lit tonight and each lantern eats 4 jars" — the total is not given; the child must interpret what to compute and pack from a dome of 48, discovering they are short and reporting the shortfall. Escalate the fade: a light meter drains across all three rounds and drains faster after each spill. Capture the first arrangement chosen in Round 1 before the constraint reveal, every commitment and reversal, and the child's stated reason. Ask nothing that repeats 6×4=24, 5×6=30, or an answer of 7. Keep total runtime near two minutes of real decisions; no praise animation longer than the decision it follows. Assignment: Festival Team Challenge. Academic construct to preserve: Lab Learner transfers equal-groups, missing-factor, and word-problem multiplication to unseen contexts at ceiling accuracy when the number pairs resemble rehearsed ones; the open question is whether that reasoning survives when a total admits several valid factor pairs and only a stated physical constraint selects the right one, and whether he re-plans rather than re-runs when the constraint changes mid-task. This node must test unseen synthesis: combine the construct in a context not practised before. Author fresh items. These have already been seen and must not be reused verbatim: math.multiplication.equal_groups, math.multiplication.missing_factor, math.multiplication.word_problem_interpretation, unseen.math.multiplication.equal_groups, unseen.math.multiplication.missing_factor, unseen.math.multiplication.word_problem_interpretation. Planner decision behind this node: Prediction was accuracy 0.70–1.00 on fresh unassisted transfer items; the Quest 'The Lantern Ferry Won't Wait' returned 3/3 correct, unassisted, exposure=unseen, provenance=independent_probe, with no confounds — accuracy 1.00, inside the preregistered band. Predicted factor-pair overgeneralization did not appear. But the theory's sharpest clause is still untested: no Quest item presented a total with multiple valid factor pairs where only a situational constraint selects the right one, and all three responses (6×4=24, 7, 5×6=30) mirror the rehearsed baseline answers exactly, so identical surface numbers remain a live alternative explanation. Transfer is supported at the evidence limit of independent performance; synthesis under constraint is unproven, which is exactly what a Boss must probe. Created at: 2026-08-08T19:10:33.621Z.

design.stakes: The swarm is finite and shrinkable. A wrong arrangement spills fireflies that fly out of the dome permanently, so the total the child must work with in the next round is smaller than it should have been — the mistake follows them. The light meter drains throughout and drains faster after each spill, so hesitation and error both cost. If the meter empties, the cart never reaches the bridge and the run ends in darkness: the child sees the unlit lanterns and the number of fireflies they lost. What is at risk is the resource the whole task depends on, and losing it means finishing the run with a visibly worse world than the one they started in.
design.failureMode: Two distinct failures, both real and both reachable. Spill failure: an unequal or incomplete arrangement dumps fireflies, permanently reducing the swarm for later rounds. Darkness failure: the light meter empties before the cart is loaded — the run ends there, the bridge stays dark, and the score is the fireflies lost. A child can complete all three rounds and still finish in darkness. Retry restarts from the full swarm, so the loss is total and clean rather than partially forgiven mid-run.
design.escalation: Round 1 gives a total with many valid factor pairs and reveals the shelf constraint only after commitment — the child learns, at cost, that arithmetic alone is not enough. Round 2 states the constraint first and hides a factor, so the reasoning must run forward under a faster-draining meter and a swarm already thinned by Round 1. Round 3 removes the total entirely: only a sentence about lanterns and jars, requiring the child to decide what to multiply, then confront a shortfall and report its size while the meter is nearly empty. Constraint arrives late, then early, then must be constructed by the child.
design.mechanicSpec: The child's finger drags fireflies from the glass dome onto jars, and pinches a jar-count dial at the cart's edge to add or remove jars. Dragging one firefly to a jar auto-mirrors the same count into every other jar on the cart, so the equal-groups rule is felt in the fingers: raise one jar to 7 and all jars jump to 7 together, and the dome's remaining count ticks down live. When the arrangement is exact, the jars flare and the cart wheels roll one shelf-length forward. On failure the jars that are over-filled crack — fireflies stream up off the top of the screen, the dome's count drops permanently, the light meter's drain rate visibly speeds up, and the cart rolls backward. In Round 3 no total is shown at all; the bridgekeeper's note sits pinned to the cart and the dome is sealed until the child taps the number of jars they've decided the order requires.
design.mathematicalHook: 42 fireflies can be packed six different honest ways and every one of them is correct arithmetic — the cart still rejects five of them. The whoa is that the shelf, not the multiplication, decides the answer: the child discovers that a fact family is a set of possibilities and the world is what picks one. And 42 refuses to split into equal jars of 5 or 8 at all, which lands the idea that some totals simply cannot be shared evenly — a first real look at factors as a property of a number rather than a thing you choose.
